papers.full_text: How to best allocate resources to combat the threat of pathogen emergence remains an important open question. Using archetypes that characterize the link from genotype to fitness in both zoonotic reservoirs and humans, we show that, across a range of plausible conditions, emergences of pathogens with pandemic potential in humans are unlikely to be preceded by detectable, failed, attempts. Yet, the number of “failed” emergence events contains information about the emergence potential of zoonotic pathogens, and should modify our beliefs about the underlying fitness landscape. Our work suggests that the most important, modifiable, risk factors for emergence may be phenomena that alter fitness landscapes, such as viral ecology in bridge species and human immunological landscapes. MATERIALS AND METHODSExpanded methods with embedded code are available in the Supplementary Materials.Calculation of prevalence in zoonotic speciesTo estimate the prevalence of viruses within zoonotic populations with a specific number of the critical mutations needed for efficient spread in the human population, we construct a fitness graph for each virus with the array of possible signatures of critical mutations (increasing, flat, and declining). We then run the system of difference equations corresponding to this graph to equilibrium, thereby obtaining the estimated background prevalence of each of the mutational signatures in the animal reservoir.In more detail,1. We construct a vector of viral fitnesses, w of length 2N, where N is the number of critical mutations that must be present for spread in the human population (for illustration, we set N = 5). Each of the entries in this vector corresponds to a bit signature where 1 indicates the presence of a particular critical mutation and 0 indicates absence. Hence, indexing from 0, each number in the array corresponds to a bit signature (e.g., for 5, in binary 00101, corresponds to the presence of the first and third required mutations), and the array entry corresponds to the relative fitness of a virus with that signature (see functions in PrevalenceCalculatingFunctions.R).2. We then construct a matrix of transition probabilities Δ to and from states with a particular mutation probability. Under a very simple model of molecular evolution, where a single base mutation is needed at each site, this gives entries in Δδij=(1−34m)x11×(1−14m)x00×(14m)x01×(34m)x10where δij is the rate of movement between sequence state i and sequnce state j, m is the per-site mutation rate, x11 denotes the number of critical mutations present in both i and j, x00 is the number absent in both i and j, x01 is the number absent from i and present in j, and x10 is the number present in i and absent in j.3. We then construct a system of difference equations such thatyt+1=ytΔw∑(ytΔw)and run it until equilibrium, defined as max(∣yi,t+1−yi,t∣<ε).Below, we apply this to each of the zoonotic evolutionary patterns of fitness (increasing, flat, and declining), assuming that selection pressure is weak when present.Bayesian updating based on failed emergencesWithin a Bayesian framework, we take the probabilities calculated above to help us understand how observed viral introductions into humans that fail to lead to emergence should change our beliefs about the likely evolutionary conditions and underlying prevalence of various mutation patterns in the zoonotic species.Posterior probability of fitness landscapes.We want to calculate the probability of different fitness landscape combinations given a number of failed emergences. Using the probabilities calculated above for emergence under various fitness patterns and our assumptions about the distribution of viral population sizes in humans, we can use Bayesian inference to understand what underlying fitness landscapes are most likely.We treat each pair of fitness landscapes (e.g., human fitness landscape A, zoonotic fitness landscape b) as a hypothesis, with equal probability of being true before the observation of a failed emergence. Using standard Bayesian approaches, in the rstan package, we obtain a posterior distribution of probabilities based on the chances of seeing x failed emergence attempts under each.Specifically, we assume that the observed number of failures X follows a binomial distributionX∼BINOM(1−ρi,X)where ρi is the probability of successful emergence under fitness landscape hypothesis i (e.g., zoonotic landscape a and human landscape B). Emergence probablities, ρi, are calculated through simulation as detailed in the analysis above and under the assumption that the number of viral replications in a human host follows a normal distribution on a log 10 scale with a mean of 9 and a standard deviation of 2. Functionally, we assume we have a set of beliefs about the probability of each hypothesis being true, pi, with a prior distribution ofp∼Dirichlet(α)where αi=1/9. We then use standard MCMC techniques to estimate the posterior distribution of pi with the simplified overall observation probability (given a belief) ofX∼BINOM(1−∑iρipi,X)It should be noted that while we illustrate our results using a relatively simple set of canonical hypotheses, this same approach could be used for any arbitrary number of hypotheses with arbitrary complexity.Posterior probability of zoonotic prevalenceWe can use the same approach under assumptions about the human landscape of fitness of emergence in human populations (here, assuming pattern B) to update our beliefs about the patterns of zoonotic prevalence under a prior assumption that prevalence follows the patterns suggested by neutral mutation (pattern b). We use the same basic approach as above, except that ρi now represents the probability of emergence in human fitness regime B given we start with i necessary mutations present, and pi now represents the assumed prevalence of virions with i mutations in the zoonotic host population. RESULTSMost of the successful pandemic viruses of the genomic sequencing era were only detected after they had achieved their pandemic potential (Table 1). Upon detection, both H1N1pdm and SARS-CoV-2 had the full complement of traits required for supercritical human-to-human transmission (i.e., R was already greater than 1). Meanwhile, pathogens detected during self-limited chains of transmission have generally failed to manifest as a serious threat. Mpox is an exception: Stuttering chains of transmission following cessation of smallpox vaccination (12) were reported for years before suspected endemicity in Nigeria in 2017 (13). The same mpox clade (clade II) later spread globally, with a concentration in MSM (men who have sex with men) populations, leading the WHO to declare a public health emergency of international concern in 2022 (14). However, it appears likely that the global spread of mpox has been driven by reduced immunity due to discontinuation of smallpox vaccination (15) and introduction of the disease to high-risk networks, rather than genetic change in the virus (more on this later) (16).Table 1.List of pandemic pathogens (left) and spillover viruses (right).Only mpox appears in both categories [we do not include Zika, as it was endemic to human populations in Africa before global spread (36)].“Successful” pandemic viruses*Spillover virusesH1N1pdmSARS-CoV-1†SARS-CoV-2MERS-CoV Mpox ‡ NipahEbolaHendra virus Mpox Influenza (H5N1, H7N9, H9N2, etc.)*HIV is not included because, though it was detected in the genomic era, it was already widespread and had emerged before this era (37).†Technically pandemic but quickly died out, likely due to effective control of hospital transmission (38).‡Concentrated in specific subpopulations and long-term trajectory unclear (14).Emergence on archetypal fitness landscapesPandemic pathogens emerge from populations of viruses evolving on interrelated fitness landscapes in humans and zoonotic hosts (17). Mutations needed for successful transmission in humans may have varying impacts on transmission in primary zoonotic hosts and/or intermediate hosts (referred to as bridge species), and clusters of mutations may interact in complex ways. Taking the example of avian influenza, at minimum three phenotypic changes are required to enable this virus to efficiently transmit between humans: First, the viral polymerase must be altered to allow the virus to exploit human cell machinery; second, a change in hemagglutinin (HA) is required for the virus to bind strongly to human cell surfaces in the upper respiratory tract; and third, changes in the HA protein are required to prevent destruction during airborne transmission (18). These phenotypic changes require multiple genetic mutations, each of which may interfere with the others. Some, such as shifts in HA binding, are likely to have negative impacts in the primary zoonotic host (18).To broadly characterize the emergence process, these complex landscapes can be reduced to a few archetypal patterns in human hosts (Fig. 1, A to C) and in the reservoir (Fig. 1, a to c). The mutations necessary for a virus to achieve criticality (represented by the red dot) might gradually increase viral fitness in humans as each mutation is acquired (a fitness hill, Fig. 1A), have a neutral fitness impact until the full complement of mutations is achieved (a fitness cliff, Fig. 1B), or even be individually detrimental until all are present (a fitness valley, Fig. 1C). Likewise, in the zoonotic host, each of these mutations could improve fitness (Fig. 1a), have a neutral impact on fitness (Fig. 1b), or decrease fitness (Fig. 1c). Of course, far more complex patterns are possible. In the human population, in particular, evolution might proceed in a variety of ways contingent on patterns of within and between host selection (19), and our framing effectively collapses many dimensions onto a single axis. To simplify the problem, we consider a virus that needs five mutations to achieve its pandemic potential in humans. Under an assumption of a fitness cliff (Fig. 1B) where mutations have a neutral impact in humans until the full complement is acquired, the probability of achieving criticality after infecting a human host if the virus has four of the five needed mutations nears 100% at viral populations in the range seen in human infections (Fig. 2B, see Materials and Methods) (22, 23). If the infecting virus has three of the five needed mutations, reaching criticality is less certain, but is almost assured at viral loads at the higher end of what is seen in human infections. However, if the virus has two or fewer of the necessary mutations, the probability of reaching criticality in a small number of human infections is almost zero. This relationship holds for both fitness hills and fitness valleys (patterns A and C), though the possibility of emergence is increased in the former and reduced in the latter (figs. S1 to S3).Fig. 2.Probabilities of acquiring a set of five mutations needed for emergence under a neutral fitness landscape in the zoonotic host (Fig. 1a) and a fitness “cliff” (Fig. 1B) in humans.(A) The number of virions that occur in primary zoonotic hosts will likely be greater than 1020 (assuming on the order of 1010 infections with 1010 viral replications per infection), and approximately 10% of these virions will have at least three of the mutations needed for emergence in humans (order >1019 virions). By contrast, absent widespread circulation, we expect only 109 to 1012 virions to be present in humans based on the viral load of individual infections. Given a fitness cliff landscape, this probability is near 100% if four needed mutations are already present at typical viral loads for single infections; if three mutations are present, the probability will range from 0% to 100% depending on the viral load of the infection; and is near 0% across the range of reasonable viral loads if two or fewer mutations are present. S5 for a log scale version of (B).Conversely, the sheer number of virions in zoonotic reservoirs versus human spillover hosts implies that potentially pandemic strains are far more likely to evolve in the zoonotic host unless selected against (tables S1 to S3). First, consider the example where the mutations needed to reach criticality in humans have a neutral fitness impact in zoonotic hosts (Fig. 1B). In this case, we expect 1.6% of the viruses in the zoonotic reservoir to be within at least one mutation of criticality (i.e., have four or more of the needed mutations, Fig. 2A), and almost 10% will have three or more of the required mutations. As a result, there is about a 10% chance under these conditions that a zoonotic infection would lead to near immediate emergence (figs. S1 to S5), an event roughly 450 times more likely than a human being infected with a virus with two or fewer required mutations and that virus evolving the required mutations (under the same conditions). This suggests that emergence might happen in several locations simultaneously, leading to a range of further challenges (24), although the evidence for this is so far minimal.A Bayesian approach to assessing emergence riskConsidering these results in a Bayesian framework leads us to conclude that repeated self-limiting chains of transmission in humans should reduce our concern about particular viral lineages, not increase it (25). That is, each spillover event that does not lead to efficient human-to-human transmission of a virus reduces our estimate of the number of virions in the zoonotic reservoir that are on the edge of criticality. Rabies provides a concrete, if extreme, example of this logic: After millions of infections in humans over the centuries, no one worries about rabies’ efficient human-to-human spread. In a simple example (see the Supplementary Materials for details), suppose that before seeing any failed emergence events, we consider all archetypical human and animal fitness landscapes to be equally likely (i.e., each combination has a probability of 0.1111). Once we reach 100 failed attempts, our posterior beliefs are such that positive and neutral selection in the zoonotic host are viewed as exceedingly unlikely (Fig. 3C) and we begin to discount the possibility of positive or neutral selection for pandemic mutations in human hosts. full_text_sections.abstract: How to best allocate resources to combat the threat of pathogen emergence remains an important open question. Using archetypes that characterize the link from genotype to fitness in both zoonotic reservoirs and humans, we show that, across a range of plausible conditions, emergences of pathogens with pandemic potential in humans are unlikely to be preceded by detectable, failed, attempts. Yet, the number of “failed” emergence events contains information about the emergence potential of zoonotic pathogens, and should modify our beliefs about the underlying fitness landscape. Our work suggests that the most important, modifiable, risk factors for emergence may be phenomena that alter fitness landscapes, such as viral ecology in bridge species and human immunological landscapes.
full_text_sections.methods: MATERIALS AND METHODSExpanded methods with embedded code are available in the Supplementary Materials.Calculation of prevalence in zoonotic speciesTo estimate the prevalence of viruses within zoonotic populations with a specific number of the critical mutations needed for efficient spread in the human population, we construct a fitness graph for each virus with the array of possible signatures of critical mutations (increasing, flat, and declining). We then run the system of difference equations corresponding to this graph to equilibrium, thereby obtaining the estimated background prevalence of each of the mutational signatures in the animal reservoir.In more detail,1. We construct a vector of viral fitnesses, w of length 2N, where N is the number of critical mutations that must be present for spread in the human population (for illustration, we set N = 5). Each of the entries in this vector corresponds to a bit signature where 1 indicates the presence of a particular critical mutation and 0 indicates absence. Hence, indexing from 0, each number in the array corresponds to a bit signature (e.g., for 5, in binary 00101, corresponds to the presence of the first and third required mutations), and the array entry corresponds to the relative fitness of a virus with that signature (see functions in PrevalenceCalculatingFunctions.R).2. We then construct a matrix of transition probabilities Δ to and from states with a particular mutation probability. Under a very simple model of molecular evolution, where a single base mutation is needed at each site, this gives entries in Δδij=(1−34m)x11×(1−14m)x00×(14m)x01×(34m)x10where δij is the rate of movement between sequence state i and sequnce state j, m is the per-site mutation rate, x11 denotes the number of critical mutations present in both i and j, x00 is the number absent in both i and j, x01 is the number absent from i and present in j, and x10 is the number present in i and absent in j.3. We then construct a system of difference equations such thatyt+1=ytΔw∑(ytΔw)and run it until equilibrium, defined as max(∣yi,t+1−yi,t∣<ε).Below, we apply this to each of the zoonotic evolutionary patterns of fitness (increasing, flat, and declining), assuming that selection pressure is weak when present.Bayesian updating based on failed emergencesWithin a Bayesian framework, we take the probabilities calculated above to help us understand how observed viral introductions into humans that fail to lead to emergence should change our beliefs about the likely evolutionary conditions and underlying prevalence of various mutation patterns in the zoonotic species.Posterior probability of fitness landscapes.We want to calculate the probability of different fitness landscape combinations given a number of failed emergences. Using the probabilities calculated above for emergence under various fitness patterns and our assumptions about the distribution of viral population sizes in humans, we can use Bayesian inference to understand what underlying fitness landscapes are most likely.We treat each pair of fitness landscapes (e.g., human fitness landscape A, zoonotic fitness landscape b) as a hypothesis, with equal probability of being true before the observation of a failed emergence. Using standard Bayesian approaches, in the rstan package, we obtain a posterior distribution of probabilities based on the chances of seeing x failed emergence attempts under each.Specifically, we assume that the observed number of failures X follows a binomial distributionX∼BINOM(1−ρi,X)where ρi is the probability of successful emergence under fitness landscape hypothesis i (e.g., zoonotic landscape a and human landscape B). Emergence probablities, ρi, are calculated through simulation as detailed in the analysis above and under the assumption that the number of viral replications in a human host follows a normal distribution on a log 10 scale with a mean of 9 and a standard deviation of 2. Functionally, we assume we have a set of beliefs about the probability of each hypothesis being true, pi, with a prior distribution ofp∼Dirichlet(α)where αi=1/9. We then use standard MCMC techniques to estimate the posterior distribution of pi with the simplified overall observation probability (given a belief) ofX∼BINOM(1−∑iρipi,X)It should be noted that while we illustrate our results using a relatively simple set of canonical hypotheses, this same approach could be used for any arbitrary number of hypotheses with arbitrary complexity.Posterior probability of zoonotic prevalenceWe can use the same approach under assumptions about the human landscape of fitness of emergence in human populations (here, assuming pattern B) to update our beliefs about the patterns of zoonotic prevalence under a prior assumption that prevalence follows the patterns suggested by neutral mutation (pattern b). We use the same basic approach as above, except that ρi now represents the probability of emergence in human fitness regime B given we start with i necessary mutations present, and pi now represents the assumed prevalence of virions with i mutations in the zoonotic host population.

full_text_sections.discussion: DISCUSSIONOur analysis shows why prior spillover events that fail to spread widely may be the exception, rather than the rule, when it comes to pathogen emergence. We further show why increasing numbers of observations of such failed spillover events should lower, rather than increase, our concern that a pathogen lineage will reach pandemic potential. These results should lead us to focus on those factors that might allow pathogens to circumvent the probabilistic barriers to their emergence.Ecology and emergence riskIn our main analysis, we focused on evolutionary adaptation of viral lineages and ignored the role of ecology. Yet, ecological changes can also create the conditions necessary for supercritical transmission. A low prevalence pathogen of limited concern can become a high burden pathogen due to changes in contact patterns. For example, respiratory adenovirus infections are largely considered a negligible problem but were a chronic problem in military recruits prevaccination due to the close and sustained contact that occurs in army barracks (26). Similarly, the international spread of mpox in 2022 was associated with entry into high contact sexual networks (14). The spread of infectious disease in humans in general is likely associated with the emergence of cities and high-density populations (27). Such ecological changes might be a more frequent, more detectable, and easier-to-modify driver of emergence than viral evolution.Farming practices, habitat change, and other factors that modify animal ecology can open new evolutionary pathways, creating potential bridges from zoonotic hosts to humans (Fig. 4). The recent H5N1 crisis in the United States is a prime example. Mammalian spillovers of highly pathogenic avian influenza have been detected for years, but never before has sustained transmission in a mammalian host been documented (18). The current epidemic in dairy cattle is likely possible only because of modern milking and farming practices (28) and may provide an opportunity for the virus to find evolutionary pathways bridging fitness valleys previously preventing emergence in humans (29). Similarly, H5N1 outbreaks have occurred in high-density mink farms and resulted in mutations thought to increase pandemic potential in humans (30). While most of these ecological changes will not result in a pandemic emergence, they may substantially increase the odds, and reset our expectations about the probability of emergence derived from past self-limiting spillover events.Fig. 4.Ecological changes and pathogen emergence.Changing ecology can allow a virus with predominately zoonotic circulation (A) to overcome formerly (effectively) insurmountable barriers to emergence and cause pandemic spread. These include ecological changes that allow the virus to overcome evolutionary barriers (B) such as high density (and other) farming practices (D) that allow for circulation of the zoonotic virus in animal species where it would not be able to circulate absent these practices, potentially opening an evolutionary bridge to pandemic emergence. Immunosuppressed humans (F) may also serve as a pathway for a virus to reach its pandemic potential, by allowing for far more replications in a human host than would be seen in immunocompetent individuals, allowing the virus to overcome probabilistic barriers to emergence. The transmission landscape in humans (C) can also change due to changes in human ecology, such as shifting immunological landscapes (E) (e.g., the loss of smallpox immunity in humans) that allow viral mutants that would not be fit to effectively circulate in human hosts; and viral entry into (perhaps emergent) transmission networks (G) where it can effectively spread despite lacking the fitness to do so in the general population.This suggests that the clearest path to strengthening biosecurity against potentially pandemic pathogens is better characterizing modifiable drivers of viral ecology in zoonotic hosts, humans, and possible intermediate species. These drivers go beyond farming practices. For example, there is evidence that the interaction between land-use changes and a shifting climate lead to higher-density fruit bat populations, alongside increased viral loads due to physiological stress, potentially increasing ease of spread of Hendra virus in these populations (human-bat contact is also increasing, though we would argue that is less important) (31). This may change the zoonotic landscape of Hendra evolution and could potentially be mitigated through ecological countermeasures including habitat maintenance (32). Similarly, immunosuppression in humans is associated with chronic viral infection and may allow for viruses to reach criticality through increased (cumulative) viral population size and reducing the negative impact of some mutations (33, 34). Treatment of immunosuppression (e.g., antiretroviral therapy for HIV) reduces these opportunities (Fig. 4).Changes may not be purely ecological. In particular, altered cross-species interactions may also open new evolutionary pathways, such as infection of hosts where recombination and reassortment are possible. For example, for influenza, the sialic acid receptor in pigs is accessible to both human and avian influenza strains (35), making pigs an important host where reassortment could occur. Such recombinations and reassortments essentially result in “teleportation” across fitness valleys, allowing a virus to acquire multiple mutations in one fell swoop, thereby circumventing some of the mathematics presented above. This, among other reasons (e.g., the ability to survive outside hosts), is why our analysis is less relevant to bacteria, where transfer of mobile elements is far more common, allowing quick acquisition of critical characteristics, such as drug resistance.Limitations and final thoughtsThis work has several limitations. We focus on simplified, archetypal, fitness landscapes that do not reflect the rich landscape of pathogen evolution and may miss some situations where emergence may be more likely. However, even in those cases, the same Bayesian logic we apply suggests that we should down weight the probability that “easy” paths to emergence exist for a lineage for which we have observed failed emergences. Our analysis also collapses both within and between host processes into a single fitness landscape, and thus, we are not fully exploring the nuances how different selective pressures interact. Further, as noted, we ignore mechanisms that may allow pathogens to “teleport” across fitness valleys, and thereby more easily emerge; although here, too, beliefs about emergence risk to associate with numbers of “failed” emergence events (self-limiting spillovers) should be informed by the same Bayesian logic. Last, we only consider one form of evidence about emergence probabilities, self-limiting spillovers. Laboratory experiments and other lines of evidence may provide important information about underlying evolutionary landscapes and could be incorporated into similar probabilistic frameworks.This work provides a more nuanced appreciation of how to interpret evidence from failed emergence events and a path to reframe how we think about self-limiting chains of transmission. It is clear that failed emergence events should be investigated and curtailed, because, as illustrated by COVID-19, the costs of pandemics are huge, and any efforts that even fractionally decrease their risk are likely cost-effective. However, particularly as failed emergence events accumulate, they should not induce panic or distract from broader approaches to pandemic prevention. Likewise, any evidence that a new ecological pathway to emergence may have opened, such as sustained circulation in a new species, should raise concern—even if the new pathway has yet to cause detected infections in humans. This is particularly the case as that first infection in humans may be as likely to cause a pandemic itself as it…

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to address the challenge of predicting pandemic emergence by examining the relationship between viral fitness landscapes and the likelihood of zoonotic pathogens achieving pandemic potential.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study used a computational model to simulate the evolution of viruses on fitness landscapes, focusing on avian influenza A viruses and their potential to emerge in human populations through zoonotic spillover.
analysis.methods: The researchers constructed fitness graphs for viruses based on critical mutations required for efficient human transmission and applied Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) techniques to estimate the posterior distribution of viral prevalence and emergence probabilities.
analysis.main_results: Most successful pandemic viruses were detected only after achieving their pandemic potential, while mpox was an exception, as it spread globally due to reduced immunity and high-risk networks rather than genetic changes.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpret that the shape of fitness landscapes significantly influences the likelihood of emergence, with fitness cliffs increasing the probability of immediate emergence if most critical mutations are already present.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: These findings suggest that understanding viral fitness landscapes can improve surveillance and risk assessment for zoonotic pathogens, particularly avian influenza, by highlighting factors that alter emergence potential.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study relies on simplified models and assumptions about mutation rates and fitness landscapes, which may limit the generalizability of its conclusions. The evidence is moderate due to these modeling constraints.

analysis.summary_en: This study explores the likelihood of zoonotic pathogens, such as avian influenza A viruses, achieving pandemic potential by analyzing their evolution on fitness landscapes. It highlights that most successful pandemic viruses were only detected after they had reached their full potential, while mpox spread globally due to reduced immunity and high-risk networks rather than genetic changes. The authors suggest that fitness landscapes, particularly those with neutral or declining effects, play a crucial role in determining emergence probabilities. They emphasize that understanding these landscapes can improve surveillance and risk assessment for zoonotic pathogens. However, the study uses simplified models, which may limit the strength of its conclusions. The findings offer insights into how factors like viral ecology and human immunological landscapes can influence the emergence of pandemic viruses.

elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 该研究使用计算模型来模拟病毒在适应性景观中的作用,重点关注禽流感 A病毒及其通过人兽共患病跨物种溢出在人类种群中出现的潜力。
elements_zh.methods: 研究人员基于对高效人类传播至关重要的关键传播构建了病毒适应性图谱,并应用马尔可夫链蒙特卡洛(MCMC)技术估计了病毒患病率和暴发概率的后验分布。
elements_zh.main_results: 大多数成功的流行病毒是在达到大流行潜力后才被检测到的,而猴痘病毒是个例外,它因宿主免疫力下降和高风险网络而在全球传播,而非基因变化。
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 作者认为适应度景观的形状显著影响新出现病毒的可能性,如果大多数关键的突变已经存在,适应度悬崖会增加立即出现的概率。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 这些发现表明,理解病毒适应性景观可以提高监测和对人兽共患病病原体的危险评估,特别是禽流感,通过突出那些改变出现潜力的因素。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 该研究依赖于简化的模型和关于突变率及适应性景观的假设,这可能限制其结论的普遍适用性。由于这些建模限制,证据等级为中等。

papers.title: Molecular Surveillance Finds No Influenza A Infection in Domestic Cats in Dhaka.
papers.abstract: Influenza A virus (IAV) is a zoonotic pathogen with a broad host range, including birds, humans, and various mammalian species. Domestic cats have been documented as incidental hosts, particularly in regions with ongoing avian influenza outbreaks. Cats are important companion animals in Dhaka, Bangladesh; however, data on IAV infection in this population are limited. This study aimed to investigate the presence of IAV in domestic cats in Dhaka through molecular surveillance. A total of 50 nasal swab samples were collected from domestic cats with mild respiratory signs presented from different areas of Dhaka city. Samples were tested for IAV using real-time reverse-transcription polymerase chain reaction (qRT-PCR) targeting the matrix (M) gene. All 50 samples tested negative for IAV. No evidence of IAV infection was found within the sampled population, suggesting low or no detectable zoonotic risk from domestic cats during the study period. These findings provide baseline data on IAV surveillance in domestic cats in Dhaka. However, given the limited sample size and sampling period, larger longitudinal surveillance studies are warranted to better assess the potential for IAV spillover in high-risk settings.

A total of 50 nasal swab samples were collected from domestic cats with mild respiratory signs in different areas of Dhaka city. The samples were tested using real-time reverse-transcription polymerase chain reaction (qRT-PCR) targeting the matrix (M) gene. papers.title: Scalable near-real-time Bayesian phylogenetics for outbreaks with Delphy.
papers.abstract: Pathogen genomic analysis is central to tracking, understanding and containing outbreaks1–13, but the complexity and cost of state-of-the-art phylogenetic tools limit global access and impact. Here we introduce Delphy, an exact reformulation of Bayesian phylogenetics14–17 designed to transform its speed, scalability and accessibility while retaining Bayesian state-of-the-art accuracy. Delphy’s central data structure, an explicit mutation-annotated tree, takes advantage of the high sequence similarity of large-scale epidemic datasets18–20 for efficient tree exploration and convergence. By reproducing key analyses from recent major epidemics, including Ebola1,21, Zika2, SARS-CoV-2 (ref. 22), mpox3,4 and H5N1 (refs. 23,24), we demonstrate state-of-the-art accuracy with up to 2–3 orders of magnitude improvements in speed. Assessing Delphy’s scalability, we show that a simulated dataset of 100,000 sequences can be analysed within a day. We distribute Delphy as a client-side web application that enables local, interactive analysis of raw data on the user’s machine. Delphy automatically identifies key viral lineages and mutations, as well as their emergence and prevalence through time, with quantified uncertainties grounded in Bayesian theory. Delphy establishes Bayesian phylogenetics as a fast, accessible frontline tool for future outbreak response. Delphy makes near-real-time and scalable Bayesian phylogenetics possible for growing viral outbreaks, enabling public health bodies anywhere to analyse and react to their own data with state-of-the-art accuracy and minimal friction.

By reproducing key analyses from recent major epidemics, including Ebola1,21, Zika2, SARS-CoV-2 (ref. 22), mpox3,4 and H5N1 (refs. 23,24), we demonstrate state-of-the-art accuracy with up to 2–3 orders of magnitude improvements in speed. Assessing Delphy’s scalability, we show that a simulated dataset of 100,000 sequences can be analysed within a day. We distribute Delphy as a client-side web application that enables local, interactive analysis of raw data on the user’s machine. Delphy automatically identifies key viral lineages and mutations, as well as their emergence and prevalence through time, with quantified uncertainties grounded in Bayesian theory. Delphy establishes Bayesian phylogenetics as a fast, accessible frontline tool for future outbreak response. Delphy makes near-real-time and scalable Bayesian phylogenetics possible for growing viral outbreaks, enabling public health bodies anywhere to analyse and react to their own data with state-of-the-art accuracy and minimal friction.

Photo by Jo-Anne McArthur / Djurrattsalliansen / We Animals September 17, 2026 Washington, DC—New documents obtained by the Animal Welfare Institute (AWI) from the Utah Department of Agriculture and Food (UDAF) through a public records request confirm an outbreak of highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) on a Utah mink farm this August—the first documented HPAI outbreak in captive mink in the United States. The records suggest that neither UDAF nor the US Department of Agriculture had a response plan in place for such an event, and that important biosecurity measures (such as placing the farm under a quarantine) were not implemented once the virus was detected. AWI is calling on federal and state lawmakers to swiftly address this public health threat by phasing out mink farming in the US. The documents describe an outbreak that has been moving through the farm’s mink population since early August, with animals “dying slowly.” They reveal that the affected farm is expecting to lose 80% of its mink to the disease. UDAF officials expressed uncertainty about appropriate protocol, ultimately deciding against a quarantine because they had “no idea what the criteria would be to release it.” As one official put it, “Our only options at this point are to watch them die or get emergency vaccine approval.” The department indicated it did not plan to pursue quarantine or testing measures, reasoning that “nothing live leaves the [farm]”—a rationale that overlooks the movement of farm workers and equipment, the presence of wild animals (including migratory birds) in the area, the potential that infected mink could escape, and the risk of transmission from carcasses of mink who died from HPAI. When UDAF officials asked the USDA to authorize emergency vaccination that could protect the farm’s remaining mink, the USDA likewise failed to respond with urgency: As of September 4 (the date of the latest records received by AWI), it did not appear that any vaccines had been provided. “This outbreak of highly pathogenic avian influenza on a US mink farm poses a serious risk to humans, and these records from the Utah Department of Agriculture and Food showcase an unacceptable lack of preparation for such a hazardous event,” said Kate Dylewsky, assistant director of government affairs at AWI. “It only takes one unlucky mutation of this dangerous virus to trigger a human health crisis, and we can no longer ignore the threat posed by disease proliferation on mink farms. The failure of state and federal officials to prepare for this scenario, or to implement important biosecurity measures in response to the outbreak, demonstrates how mink farming operates with almost no oversight, compounding the threat to the public. It’s time to leave this industry in the past.” The science is well established: Mink farms are a public health hazard. Farmed mink pose a particular risk to humans because the upper respiratory tract of a mink is physiologically similar to ours, meaning a virus that mutates to thrive and spread in mink may become more dangerous to people as well. Crowded conditions on fur farms create an ideal setting for pathogens to circulate, and each additional mink that is infected creates another opportunity for the virus to mutate into something transmissible to and between humans. Over the past several years, tens of thousands of captive mink in the United States—and millions worldwide—have been infected with SARS-CoV-2, the virus that causes COVID-19, and mink-to-human transmission of variants of this virus have been reported in at least five countries. The H5N1 virus, which causes avian influenza, has also infected tens of thousands of mink on dozens of European fur farms since 2022. During an October 2022 outbreak on a mink farm in Spain, the virus gained at least one mutation that favors mammal-to-mammal spread (rather than bird-to-mammal), allowing it to proliferate among mink. Scientists called this mink farm outbreak a “clear mechanism for an H5 pandemic to start” and “a warning bell.” H5N1 infections were also detected at multiple mink farms in Finland in 2023. Concerningly, Congress is considering inclusion of language in the Farm Bill that would allow the mink farming industry to receive taxpayer dollars to develop and expand into international markets. Given the clear and urgent risks to public health associated with mink farming, it is a grave error for the Farm Bill to promote the use of public funds to keep this industry afloat. To address the public health threat of mink farming, AWI has spearheaded the introduction in Congress of the Mink: Vectors for Infection Risk in the United States Act (Mink VIRUS Act). Sponsored by Rep. Adriano Espaillat (D-NY), this bill would establish a one-year phaseout of mink fur farms in the US and create a grant program to reimburse mink farmers for the full value of their farms. This US outbreak of HPAI underscores the urgent need to enact the Mink VIRUS Act. AWI has also led the push for the Finding Urgent Relief from Vectors for Infection Risk and Unchecked Spillover (FUR VIRUS) Act in Illinois, which would implement crucial disease prevention measures by barring the establishment of new fur farms in the state. Innovation Scientists Develop Nasal H5N1 Vaccine Designed to Block Bird Flu Where the Virus Enters the Body Published Sep 15, 2026 11:00 AM EDT By Lucia Carter Editorial Illustration via AI Share on Twitter Share on Facebook Share on Pocket A nasal vaccine protected mice from a lethal strain of H5N1 and dramatically reduced the amount of virus in their noses and windpipes. The experimental vaccine gave two doses to the animals before they were exposed to the virus. All vaccinated mice survived, while those that did not receive the vaccine died. But survival was only part of the result. When researchers examined the animals' respiratory tissues, they found roughly 100,000 times less virus in the nose and trachea of vaccinated mice than in unvaccinated animals. The finding is particularly interesting because these are among the first places H5N1 can encounter the body after entering through the respiratory tract. The vaccine has not been tested in people, so it is far too early to know whether the same protection would occur in humans. Still, the results point to a different way of preparing the immune system for bird flu: meeting the virus at the respiratory surface instead of relying only on protection circulating deeper inside the body. The Vaccine Was Delivered Through the Nose Most vaccines are injected into muscle. A nasal vaccine takes a different route, coating the lining of the nose and upper airways with vaccine material. This can stimulate mucosal immunity, a type of immune defence that operates at surfaces where pathogens first enter the body. For a respiratory virus such as H5N1, researchers wanted to know whether building that local defence could help stop the virus earlier. To create the experimental vaccine, the researchers used a modified vesicular stomatitis virus, or VSV, as a carrier. The engineered virus was designed to deliver H5N1-related material and trigger an immune response without causing the disease associated with H5N1. The mice received two doses four weeks apart. Four weeks after the second dose, the researchers exposed them to a dose of H5N1 that would normally be fatal. Every Vaccinated Mouse Survived The difference was immediate. All of the vaccinated mice survived the H5N1 challenge. The unvaccinated control animals did not. The vaccinated mice also produced strong antibody responses. Some of those antibodies circulated through the body, while others were found in the respiratory tract, giving the animals immune activity close to the place where the virus was introduced. Researchers then looked more closely at where H5N1 had travelled inside the animals. That was when the nasal vaccine's most distinctive effect became apparent. The Nose and Trachea Had Far Less Virus The researchers measured viral levels in several tissues, including the nose, trachea and lungs. The vaccine substantially reduced the amount of H5N1 found in all three areas. But the reduction was particularly dramatic in the upper respiratory tract. Vaccinated mice had about 100,000 times less virus in their nasal and tracheal tissues than the unvaccinated animals. The reduction in the lungs was also substantial, although not as pronounced as in the upper airways. That pattern fits the idea behind the nasal vaccine. Rather than waiting for the immune system to respond after the virus has moved deeper into the body, the vaccine appears to establish strong local defences along the respiratory surfaces. The researchers also found that the vaccinated animals had less severe damage in their lungs and maintained better overall health after infection. The Protection Lasted for Months The researchers did not stop after the first H5N1 challenge. They wanted to see whether the protection would fade quickly. They followed another group of vaccinated mice for 250 days, measuring their immune responses over time. The animals maintained neutralising antibodies, which can prevent viruses from infecting cells. When the mice were later exposed to a lethal dose of H5N1, both vaccine doses tested again produced 100% survival. The vaccinated animals also continued to show markedly lower amounts of virus in the nose and trachea than the controls. For an experimental vaccine, that durability is notable. It suggests the nasal approach did not simply produce a short-lived burst of protection immediately after vaccination. Human Trials Will Have to Answer the Bigger Questions The findings are promising, but they come entirely from animal experiments. A vaccine that works in mice can still behave very differently in humans. Researchers will need to establish whether the modified VSV vaccine is safe, what dose would be appropriate, how well it stimulates mucosal immunity in people, and whether it can protect against H5N1 infection or severe disease. For now, the experiment offers a particularly striking result: after nasal vaccination, the mice that survived lethal H5N1 had dramatically less virus in the very tissues the virus encountered first. That makes the nose more than just the route used to deliver the vaccine. In this study, it became part of the defence. The Vaccine Was Delivered Through the Nose Most vaccines are injected into muscle. A nasal vaccine takes a different route, coating the lining of the nose and upper airways with vaccine material. This can stimulate mucosal immunity, a type of immune defence that operates at surfaces where pathogens first enter the body. For a respiratory virus such as H5N1, researchers wanted to know whether building that local defence could help stop the virus earlier. To create the experimental vaccine, the researchers used a modified vesicular stomatitis virus, or VSV, as a carrier. The engineered virus was designed to deliver H5N1-related material and trigger an immune response without causing the disease associated with H5N1. The mice received two doses four weeks apart. Four weeks after the second dose, the researchers exposed them to a dose of H5N1 that would normally be fatal. Every Vaccinated Mouse Survived The difference was immediate. All of the vaccinated mice survived the H5N1 challenge. The unvaccinated control animals did not. The vaccinated mice also produced strong antibody responses. Some of those antibodies circulated through the body, while others were found in the respiratory tract, giving the animals immune activity close to the place where the virus was introduced. Researchers then looked more closely at where H5N1 had travelled inside the animals. That was when the nasal vaccine's most distinctive effect became apparent. The Nose and Trachea Had Far Less Virus The researchers measured viral levels in several tissues, including the nose, trachea and lungs. The vaccine substantially reduced the amount of H5N1 found in all three areas. But the reduction was particularly dramatic in the upper respiratory tract. Vaccinated mice had about 100,000 times less virus in their nasal and tracheal tissues than the unvaccinated animals. The reduction in the lungs was also substantial, although not as pronounced as in the upper airways. That pattern fits the idea behind the nasal vaccine. Rather than waiting for the immune system to respond after the virus has moved deeper into the body, the vaccine appears to establish strong local defences along the respiratory surfaces. The researchers also found that the vaccinated animals had less severe damage in their lungs and maintained better overall health after infection. The Protection Lasted for Months The researchers did not stop after the first H5N1 challenge. They wanted to see whether the protection would fade quickly. They followed another group of vaccinated mice for 250 days, measuring their immune responses over time. The animals maintained neutralising antibodies, which can prevent viruses from infecting cells. When the mice were later exposed to a lethal dose of H5N1, both vaccine doses tested again produced 100% survival. The vaccinated animals also continued to show markedly lower amounts of virus in the nose and trachea than the controls. For an experimental vaccine, that durability is notable. It suggests the nasal approach did not simply produce a short-lived burst of protection immediately after vaccination. Human Trials Will Have to Answer the Bigger Questions The findings are promising, but they come entirely from animal experiments. A vaccine that works in mice can still behave very differently in humans. Researchers will need to establish whether the modified VSV vaccine is safe, what dose would be appropriate, how well it stimulates mucosal immunity in people, and whether it can protect against H5N1 infection or severe disease. For now, the experiment offers a particularly striking result: after nasal vaccination, the mice that survived lethal H5N1 had dramatically less virus in the very tissues the virus encountered first. That makes the nose more than just the route used to deliver the vaccine. In this study, it became part of the defence. news.title_zh: 科学家开发鼻腔喷雾H5N1 疫苗,旨在阻断禽流感病毒进入人体 - medicaldaily.com
news.source_body_en: Scientists have developed a nasal vaccine targeting H5N1, a strain of bird flu, which showed promising results in mice. Published on Sep 15, 2026, by medicaldaily.com, the study found that vaccinated mice were completely protected from a lethal H5N1 strain, with the virus present in their nasal and tracheal tissues at roughly 100,000 times lower levels than in unvaccinated animals. The vaccine was administered through the nose, aiming to stimulate mucosal immunity at the initial entry points of the virus. However, the vaccine has not been tested in humans, so its effectiveness in people remains uncertain. The findings suggest a potential new strategy for preparing the immune system against respiratory viruses like H5N1 by targeting the respiratory surface directly. This development is still in the experimental phase and requires further investigation before it can be considered for human use.
news.content_zh: 科学家开发了一种针对H5N1禽流感病毒的鼻腔喷雾疫苗,在小鼠中显示出有希望的结果。该研究由medicaldaily.com于2026年9月15日发布,发现接种疫苗的小鼠完全抵抗致命性H5N1病毒株,其鼻腔和气管组织中的病毒含量比未接种疫苗的小鼠低约100,000倍。该疫苗通过鼻腔给药,旨在刺激病毒最初进入人体的黏膜免疫。然而,该疫苗尚未在人类中进行测试,因此其在人类中的有效性仍不确定。研究结果表明,通过直接针对呼吸道表面,可能为准备免疫系统应对如H5N1等呼吸道病毒提供了一种新的策略。这一进展仍处于实验阶段,需进一步研究才能考虑用于人类。
news.summary_zh: 科学家开发了一种针对H5N1禽流感病毒的鼻腔喷雾疫苗,在小鼠中显示出有希望的结果。该研究由medicaldaily.com于2026年9月15日发布,发现接种疫苗的小鼠完全抵抗致命性H5N1病毒株,其鼻腔和气管组织中的病毒含量比未接种疫苗的小鼠低约100,000倍。该疫苗通过鼻腔给药,旨在刺激病毒最初进入人体的黏膜免疫。然而,该疫苗尚未在人类中进行测试,因此其在人类中的有效性仍不确定。研究结果表明,通过直接针对呼吸道表面,可能为准备免疫系统应对如H5N1等呼吸道病毒提供了一种新的策略。这一进展仍处于实验阶段,需进一步研究才能考虑用于人类。

Home Arts + Culture Economy Education Environment + Energy Ethics + Religion Health Politics + Society Science + Tech World Podcasts Local En Español Edition Africa Australia Brasil Canada Canada (français) Català España Europe France Global Indonesia New Zealand United Kingdom United States Donate Skip to content Edition: United States Africa Australia Brasil Canada Canada (français) Català España Europe France Global Indonesia New Zealand United Kingdom s Donate Newsletters Become an author Sign up as a reader Sign in Academic rigor, journalistic flair Arts + Culture Economy Education Environment + Energy Ethics + Religion Health Politics + Society Science + Tech World Podcasts Local Stephen Frink/Getty Bird flu has claimed its first Australian sea lion and dolphin. How does the virus get into these animals? Published: September 15, 2026 4:13pm EDT A rare Australian sea lion (Neophoca cinerea) on Kangaroo Island has been confirmed to have died from highly pathogenic H5N1 bird flu. The sea lion had recently been attacked by a shark, weakening it. Testing revealed the cause of death was the virus. Another dead sea lion is being tested. The first confirmed H5N1 death recorded for this species in Australia marks a significant and worrying moment for Australian wildlife. These sea lions are the rarest pinniped to breed on our coasts. They’re considered endangered, as their population is under 12,000. This species of sea lion breeds slowly, meaning even a limited outbreak of bird flu could be very bad news for breeding colonies. The strain of bird flu now circulating in Australia and New Zealand has evolved to infect some mammal species as well as birds. Since 2021, it has decimated some seals and sea lion species overseas, especially in South America. The virus is even capable of infecting and killing dolphins. But how does the virus pass between these animals? How do seals and dolphins actually get the infection? There’s much we don’t know. But here’s what we do. Bird (and mammal) flu? The highly pathogenic H5N1 strain of bird flu (avian influenza) was first detected in 1996. Highly pathogenic means it is capable of causing severe disease. In 2020, the virus mutated into a new, more deadly variant capable of infecting more species. It is no longer just a threat to birds. Since 2021, this strain has caused mass die-offs in pinnipeds (seals, sea lions, walruses and so on). In Argentina, more than 17,000 southern elephant seal pups died. After the virus reached Australia’s Heard Island, drone surveys identified more than 13,000 dead pups from the same species. Some pinnipeds were able to catch older bird flu strains. But these mainly affected their respiratory tracts. The newer highly pathogenic H5N1 strain can also invade the brain and nervous system of mammals. Sea lions have been found with encephalitis, brain inflammation and other neurological signs before death. In Florida, a bottlenose dolphin infected with H5N1 was found to have the highest concentration of virus in its brain. How do pinnipeds catch the virus? The way the virus gets into pinnipeds is likely from birds. When sick seabirds infected with the virus die on the islands used by sea lions for breeding, the virus can jump across to the mammal. This can be through direct contact, scavenging carcasses or exposure to contaminated sand, rocks, water, faeces or mucus. Sick birds can and do sneeze and cough, spreading viral particles. Direct transmission from mammal to mammal is suspected, though not yet conclusively proven in most wild marine mammal die-off events. But the fact so many elephant seal pups died rapidly suggests the virus is able to spread between them. Transmission between elephant seals is suspected to have occurred in Argentina. It’s highly likely that the virus can spread faster in dense seal and sea lion colonies. Pinnipeds, too, can sneeze and cough, which would help spread the virus. One researcher testing transmission reportedly had a seal sneeze in their face. They then contracted severe conjunctivitis in the eye. The bird flu virus was detected. Sea lions may be getting infected by contact with sick or dead birds and their excretions. atosan/Getty But what about whales and dolphins? So far, so logical. But how can dolphins and other cetaceans contract the virus? After a dolphin washed up dead near Goolwa, South Australia, it tested positive for H5N1 – the first case in Australia. How did it happen? SA chief veterinary officer Dr Skye Fruean told the ABC it was likely the dolphin had “eaten a bird or interacted closely with a wild bird”. This is possible, but we don’t know for sure. What we do know is that this H5N1 strain has been found in a range of dolphin species around the world. So far, there’s little evidence of large whales being infected with bird flu. A juvenile dead whale washed ashore at Victor Harbour was found not to have the virus. Dolphins are likely to get infected by contact with sick birds. Damian Lugowski/Getty How long can the virus survive in the environment? Viruses can survive outside a host, though typically not for long. The H5N1 influenza virus generally survives longest in cool, moist conditions. It can remain infectious for days and sometimes weeks in water, depending on temperature, salinity and sunlight. In hot, dry environments, survival is much shorter. Carcasses can act as temporary reservoirs of the virus while tissues remain fresh. This is one reason why beaches and breeding colonies can be transmission hotspots during an outbreak. What can we do? There’s no real way to stop the spread of H5N1 now that it’s here. But there are many ways we can reduce its impact. Removing carcasses safely is crucial, as it removes these viral reservoirs and stops it getting into Australia’s many scavenging animals. Investing in better monitoring and detection is essential if we are to slow the spread by helping us to target affected populations. We must ramp up protection for endangered species, reduce human pressures such as disturbance of seal colonies and plan to help depleted populations recover. Ultimately, the death of this sea lion shows us that the burden of bird flu will reach far beyond birds. This strain of the virus is a wide-ranging threat able to affect entire ecosystems. We must do what we can to protect them. Conservation Environment Seals Viruses Bird flu Virus transmission Pinnipeds Want to write? FFAR Research to Test Fogging Approach to Reduce Avian Influenza Transmission Researchers are testing an innovative, plant-based approach to reduce transmission of avian influenza PUBLISHED ON September 15, 2026 Avian influenza has severe economic consequences for the U.S. poultry and egg industries. The virus spreads rapidly among birds and leads to mass depopulation of infected flocks. (Photo by Andrey Tikhonovskiy on Unsplash) Discover more Health Consult Online Doctors Bird INDIANAPOLIS, Ind. — H5N1 influenza, commonly known as bird flu, continues to threaten U.S. poultry and egg production. The Foundation for Food & Agriculture Research (FFAR) and Entomol Products, LLC are investing $448,940 in a Rapid Outcomes from Agricultural Research (ROAR) grant to test an innovative, plant-based approach to reduce transmission of avian influenza. Researchers are determining whether intermittently fogging or misting hydrogenated catmint oil (HCO), a product with demonstrated antiviral properties, in poultry housing can interrupt transmission of avian influenza viruses. Avian influenza has severe economic consequences for the U.S. poultry and egg industries. The virus spreads rapidly among birds and leads to mass depopulation of infected flocks. This influenza virus is classified as High or Low Pathogenic Avian Influenza based on how it affects poultry. Highly pathogenic avian influenza viruses cause severe disease and high mortality in infected poultry, while low pathogenic avian influenza is a mild or asymptomatic viral infection. “Producers need practical solutions to reduce avian influenza transmission that work with existing infrastructure to protect their flocks and limit losses,” said Dr. Jasmine Bruno, FFAR scientific program director. “As fogging is a widely used practice in poultry houses, we want to know if it’s a promising mechanism for protecting birds.” HCO is a modified plant essential oil and an EPA-registered active ingredient used in commercially available insect repellents. Previous research found that aerosolized formulations containing HCO significantly reduced H1N1 influenza virus in the air. Led by Dr. David Hallahan, chief science officer at Entomol, and Dr. Ekramy Sayedahmed, assistant professor of poultry medicine at Purdue University, researchers are testing whether HCO can reduce avian influenza transmission. The researchers are using low pathogenic avian influenza to evaluate HCO’s antiviral effects against avian influenza and inform its potential application against highly pathogenic avian influenza. The team is also establishing effective aerosol delivery parameters, including HCO concentration, fogging duration and frequency, effective range and overall efficacy. “Entomol’s hydrogenated catmint oil technology has demonstrated the ability to disrupt influenza viruses in the air and on surfaces at very low concentrations, said Dr. Hallahan. “This FFAR-supported project will allow us to rigorously evaluate its potential as a practical biosecurity tool for poultry producers.” Discover more Book Wildlife Safaris Choose Bird Feeders HEALTH FFAR is investing in this research to support the U.S. Department of Agriculture’s research priority on Increasing Profitability of Farmers and Ranchers. This research aims to develop a practical, science-driven intervention that strengthens national readiness for avian influenza outbreaks and protects U.S. poultry producers’ livelihoods. FFAR’s ROAR program rapidly funds research and outreach in response to emerging or unanticipated threats to the U.S. food supply or agricultural systems. Foundation for Food & Agriculture Research The Foundation for Food & Agriculture Research (FFAR) builds public-private partnerships to fund bold research addressing big food and agriculture challenges. FFAR was established in the 2014 Farm Bill to increase public agriculture research investments, fill knowledge gaps and complement the U.S. Department of Agriculture’s research agenda. FFAR’s model matches federal funding from Congress with private funding, delivering a powerful return on taxpayer investment.
