supplementary_news.content_title: Bird Flu’s Dairy Cow Disguise Finally Explained
supplementary_news.content: Close Menu Facebook X (Twitter) Instagram Biology Chemistry Earth Health Physics Science Space Technology Facebook X (Twitter) Pinterest YouTube RSS Home»Health»Bird Flu’s Dairy Cow Disguise Finally Explained Health Bird Flu’s Dairy Cow Disguise Finally Explained By University of PittsburghSeptember 16, 2026No Comments5 Mins Read Facebook Twitter Pinterest Telegram LinkedIn WhatsApp Email Reddit Share Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Telegram Email Reddit Scientists finally uncovered the biological trick that allowed H5N1 bird flu to hide in dairy cows and spread before anyone knew what was happening. Credit: Shutterstock The study reveals the biology behind why the disease appeared so different after spreading to cows and offers a framework for recognizing new forms of the disease more quickly. H5N1 bird flu caused severe infections in cows’ udders while largely sparing their lungs when it began spreading among U.S. dairy cattle in early 2024. That pattern made the disease difficult to recognize. In other mammalian species, H5N1 affects the lungs. Researchers at the University of Pittsburgh School of Public Health have now traced that difference to the molecular structures the virus uses to attach to cells. The structures that allowed H5N1 to bind were abundant in udder tissue but nearly absent from cows’ airways. Published in Science Advances, the study provides the first explanation of the biological mechanism behind this pattern. Why H5N1 favored cows’ udders For influenza viruses, the ability to infect a particular animal or organ depends partly on finding compatible receptors on its cells. These receptors include certain glycans, sugar-based molecules that interact with the virus much like a lock and key. Suresh Kuchipudi, Ph.D., the study’s senior author and chair of Infectious Diseases and Microbiology at Pitt Public Health, has spent his career studying influenza, with a particular focus on how receptor biology shapes infection. But standard methods for detecting receptors had left an unresolved question in cattle. Earlier studies by other groups used staining techniques to identify flu-related glycan receptors in cows’ noses, tracheas, and lungs. Their presence did not explain why the animals were largely escaping respiratory infection. The researchers needed to determine which of those receptors H5N1 could actually use. Microscopic image of bovine mammary gland tissue showing influenza virus receptors (yellow) on mammary epithelial cells. The study identified receptor patterns that may help explain the susceptibility of the bovine mammary gland to H5N1 infection and its ability to support viral replication. Credit: Department of Infectious Diseases and Microbiology, School of Public Health, University of Pittsburgh “Glycan biology is very complex,” said Kuchipudi. “We realized that, to understand what was really going on, we would need to use more innovative technologies and map out the fine‐detailed architecture that enables the virus to bind to cells.” Kuchipudi collaborated with Lauren E. Pepi, Ph.D., of Harvard Medical School, an expert in glycomics, the comprehensive cataloging of glycan structures. The team combined experiments that tested viral binding with staining methods and ultra-high-resolution imaging to examine the receptors in greater detail. In those experiments, only a particular subtype, called N-linked sialic acid receptors, could bind to H5N1. Their distribution explained the contrast between the airways and udders. These receptors were virtually absent from cow airway tissue but widespread in udders, making them a “perfect breeding ground for the virus,” Kuchipudi said. Udder infections delayed H5N1’s detection That preference for udder tissue helps explain the difficulty veterinarians faced when the disease first appeared in dairy cattle along the Texas Panhandle. The animals developed persistent cases of severe, necrotizing mastitis, a painful inflammation that damages tissue in the mammary glands, where milk is produced. “Mastitis is a classic disease in milk-production animals, and veterinarians were dutifully looking to all the usual suspects for the source, like bacterial pathogens,” said Kuchipudi. “When the real culprit turned out to be bird flu, everyone in the field was caught completely by surprise. We hadn’t even remotely considered that cattle could be a host for H5N1.” Dr. Suresh Kuchipudi, Ph.D., chair of Infectious Diseases and Microbiology at the University of Pittsburgh School of Public Health. Credit: University of Pittsburgh School of Public Health During the weeks before H5N1 was identified, the virus spread between herds, sickening cattle and contaminating their surroundings. Infection in the udders also created a route for the virus to leave the animals through their milk. “If a cow is infected, it sheds a lot of virus into the milk,” said Kuchipudi. “This raised concerns about occupational risk for farm workers. Also, there is a habit of feeding raw milk to domestic pets, like cats, and there have been instances of cats dying, which we studied previously.” Pasteurization effectively kills the virus, Kuchipudi emphasized, underscoring the importance of avoiding raw milk. Receptors could flag other vulnerable hosts H5N1 now affects more than 100 bird and mammal species worldwide. The researchers propose using their approach to assess whether other species could become hosts and which tissues might be vulnerable. Recognizing an unfamiliar pattern of infection sooner could give public health officials more time to take measures to limit its spread. “We can preemptively screen different species and different tissues within them for susceptibility,” said Kuchipudi. “For example, would they exhibit respiratory symptoms? Would they show only mastitis, as in cows? Or would they show neurological disease, as our team has shown in cats? The lessons learned could potentially help prevent us from being caught by surprise again.” Reference: “Receptor basis of unusual tissue tropism of avian influenza H5N1 clade 2.3.4.4b virus in cattle” by Surabhi Srinivas, Shubhada K. Chothe, Santhamani Ramasamy, Sougat Misra, Noel Chandan Nallipogu, Lindsey LaBella, Yin-Ting Yeh, May Wang, Lauren E. Pepi, Heidi L. Pecoraro, Brett T. Webb and Suresh V. Kuchipudi, 19 June 2026, Science Advances. DOI: 10.1126/sciadv.aea2068 This research was supported by Pitt Public Health, and the U.S. Department of Agriculture’s National Institute of Food and Agriculture (FP00039373/AWD00010780). Photograph: Brad Leue/Alamy First H5 bird flu death of endangered Australian sea lion recorded amid fears for small population South Australian authorities say case discovered on Kangaroo Island is first for species of which less than 12,000 animals remain Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast South Australia has recorded the first death of an endangered Australian sea lion from H5 bird flu. Experts say about 12,000 Australian sea lions remain – though a more recent estimate put the figure at less than 10,000. Most of the population are found in South Australia, with the remainder in Western Australia. On Sunday, the state’s environment minister, Emily Bourke, said the sea lion was found dead at Seal Bay on Kangaroo Island, the third-largest single colony. “We’ve seen quite a number of mammal cases, but the Australian sea lion is the rarest seal found in our Australian waters,” Bourke said. “85% of the population is found here in South Australia. It’s an endangered species.” She said the sea lion had been recovering from a shark attack, but that bird flu had caused its death. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email “We found that it was actually not the shark attack that killed the sea lion. It was the bird flu ... we might find that this particular case was more susceptible because it was recovering.” The government said the sea lion had first been observed with the shark wound three months ago and had been monitored since that time. Tests had returned a strong positive result for H5 bird flu and the government said it was confident the shark wound had not caused its death. There had been no other known endangered sea lion deaths at Seal Bay, but the population was being closely monitored. Bourke said there was “no real” mammal vaccine that “you could get off the shelf at the moment”. “It was used in cattle in the US and they did an experimental trial in Hawaii on their monk seals, which they have seen that has been successful,” Bourke said. “We have been working very closely with the federal government to highlight that we are willing and able to participate in a trial here in South Australia.” Seal Bay has an estimated 800 Australian sea lions. skip past newsletter promotion after newsletter promotion Australia has just 12,000 sea lions left – and ‘carnage’ may await them as bird flu takes hold, scientists warn Read more Bourke said the population was already diminishing by 2% every year, even before the arrival of bird flu, which will have a “devastating impact” on population levels if no vaccine can be administered. “We’ve seen Heard Island [that there has been] a reduction in the population there for our seal pups by 75%. They were impacted by bird flu,” she said. “And we’ve seen other experiences around the world where they were impacted by 95%. We know that this is going to be not the first and only case of [the virus] going into our sea lions.” Last month, John Woinarski, a leading mammal scientist at Charles Darwin University, told Guardian Australia that he feared the virus would quickly start affecting more seals and sea lions. “The carnage may be substantial and represent a serious conservation impact,” he said. “I fear for Australian sea lions in particular because of their small population size. “It’s likely in the next few weeks it will spread more quickly into the sea lion population in South Australia generally because of the proximity of the sea lion colonies to breeding seabird colonies or affected seabirds.” H5 bird flu has already affected pinnipeds in South America and sub-Antarctica, where it has caused catastrophic losses in populations of some species, particularly among pups. SA had confirmed Australia’s first case in a mainland mammal in August, after a dead long-nosed fur seal found at Beachport on the Limestone Coast tested positive for H5N1. Add Yahoo on Google BARRON COUNTY, Wis., (WLAX, WEUX) - The Wisconsin Department of Agriculture, Trade and Consumer Protection has confirmed that a case of highly pathogenic avian influenza has been found in a commercial poultry flock in Barron County. https://www.facebook.com/20531316728/posts/10154009990506729/ DATCP says they are working with the U.S. Department of Agriculture to response to this case, with premises being quarantined. Officials add that birds on the property were depopulated to prevent the spread, ensuring that birds from this flock will not enter the food system. 南澳环境部长伯克说,过去的星期五在袋鼠岛南部发现一只海狮死亡,检测后证实它体内有H5N1禽流感病毒。(法新社资料图片) 澳洲首次在海狮身上验出H5N1型禽流感病毒。 南澳环境部长伯克说,过去的星期五在袋鼠岛南部发现一只海狮死亡,检测后证实它体内有H5N1禽流感病毒。当局的数据显示,全澳洲至今证实521宗动物感染H5N1禽流感的个案,当中大约一半在南澳。 5 2 0 2 0 1 澳大利亚首次在濒危海狮身上验出高致病性H5N1禽流感病毒。南澳州环境部门表示,于袋鼠岛(Kangaroo Island)附近海豹湾(Seal Bay)发现一头澳大利亚海狮(Australian sea lion)死亡,经检测确定带有H5N1禽流感病毒。目前,澳大利亚海狮数量大约剩下12,000头,有专家更估计或少于10,000头。 图为澳大利亚袋鼠岛(Kangaroo Island)的澳大利亚海狮 (Australian sea lion)。(Getty Images) 南澳州环境部门称,约85%澳大利亚海狮栖息于南澳大利亚,属于濒危物种,其中海豹湾估计有约800头。 当局表示,该头死亡海狮于11日被发现。牠约3个月因曾被鲨鱼袭击受伤,之后一直受到监测。当局经检测认为,其死亡并非由于伤口,而是因期间感染禽流感。当局表示,担心禽流感威胁澳大利亚海狮生存,令其进一步濒危。 澳大利亚确认首宗本土H5N1禽流感个案 菲律宾家禽爆疫情澳大利亚出现首宗本土H5N1禽流感个案中国解除西班牙家禽进口禁令 允许非疫区禽类及其产品输华日本首都圈确认发生高致病性禽流感 23:01更新:2026-07-10 23:01 在Google 追踪《香港01》 讚好 2 2 0 0 0 0 澳大利亚7月10日确认首宗本土H5N1禽流感个案,造成一只海鸟死亡,外界担忧病毒自上个月传入澳大利亚后,可能开始进一步扩散。另外菲律宾家禽也爆发H5N1禽流感疫情。 这是澳大利亚本土海鸟首次确诊感染该病毒,此前所有个案均发生在迁移的海鸟身上,个案总数达到12宗。 澳大利亚国旗 (Getty Images) 澳大利亚农业部长哥连斯(Julie Collins)表示事态发展令人担忧,但目前尚无证据显示有大规模死亡,或病毒已扩散至其他动物族群、家禽或农业领域。 哥连斯上月称,西澳州省(Western Australia)南部勒格兰角国家公园(Cape Le Grand national park)6月中发现一只棕色贼鸥(brown skua)不适,其后不治。 图为棕色贼鸥(brown skua)。(Getty Images) 菲律宾也出现H5N1病毒,世界动物卫生组织(WOAH)周五表示,菲律宾东方民都洛省(Oriental Mindoro)家禽中爆发H5N1禽流感疫情。 组织引述菲律宾部门报告称,在卡帕兰镇的一群39只家禽中检测到H5N1病毒,作为预防措施,家禽随后已被扑杀。 禽流感|美国全球首宗人类感染H5N5个案 Topics & Projects Antimicrobial Stewardship Chronic Wasting Disease Osterholm Update Podcasts Newsletters About CIDRAP CIDRAP in the News Our Staff Our Director Osterholm in the Press Shop Merchandise Contact Us About Search CLOSE Search Support Menu Avian flu detected in Minnesota turkeys, US waterfowl News brief Stephanie Soucheray, MA Topics Avian Influenza (Bird Flu) Share Copied to clipboard Myles Tan / Flickr cc The US Department of Agriculture (USDA) Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service (APHIS) noted three major H5N1 avian flu outbreaks at Minnesota facilities this past week. Two commercial turkey operations in Big Stone County and Becker County had 55,700 and 44,400 birds affected, respectively. A commercial poultry breeder facility in Otter Tail County also reported an outbreak hitting 18,000 birds. In the past 30 days, 16 confirmed flocks have tested positive for highly pathogenic avian influenza, including 10 commercial flocks and six backyard flocks. Roughly 400,000 birds have been affected. Multiple wild-bird detections in Indiana, Utah In other APHIS news, wild bird detections have increased this month, with almost 30 detections in Kootenai County, Indiana, and 20 detections in Webber County, Utah. Other states have also noted a smaller number of cases. All recent wild bird detections are in mallards or other waterfowl. Airport air sampling captures COVID, influenza viruses News brief Mary Van Beusekom, MS Topics COVID-19 Influenza, General Lya_Cattel / iStock Air sampling at four US airports in 2023 and 2024 detected SARS-CoV-2, the virus that causes COVID-19, in over 98% of samples and influenza A in over 17%, according to a study published in PLOS Global Public Health. Researchers from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention led the study, which involved air monitoring in congregate areas at San Francisco International Airport, Newark Liberty International Airport, Washington Dulles International Airport, and Dallas/Fort Worth International Airport. The team placed samplers on tables 28 to 30 inches above the floor near customs and immigration inspection areas and international arrivals. Each ThermoFisher AerosolSense unit collected air samples for 10 hours per day, and the sample-collection cartridges were removed after 20 hours of use Monday through Thursday and 30 hours over the weekend. Correlation of the air samples with aviation wastewater, traveler nasal swabs, and national clinical surveillance data was also tested using data from two airports. Air sampling complements wastewater monitoring, the researchers said: “This approach is particularly effective for capturing respiratory pathogens from diverse populations, including asymptomatic or pre-symptomatic individuals who might not otherwise engage with clinical testing or contribute to accessible wastewater systems.” May be a component of pandemic preparedness Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) testing revealed SARS-CoV-2 in 98.3% of 463 air samples and influenza A in 17.2%. While influenza A positivity correlated with that in aviation wastewater, traveler nasal swabs, and national clinical surveillance, SARS-CoV-2 positivity didn’t align well. Detection of respiratory pathogens through air monitoring may inform targeted mitigation strategies, including enhanced ventilation, air purification, public health messaging, and allocation of public health resources. Genetic sequencing of SARS-CoV-2 from air samples identified lineages also found in wastewater samples during the same period from the same airports. In addition, it detected 30 viral species and recovered high-quality genomes for SARS-CoV-2, influenza, bocavirus (a virus that mainly causes respiratory tract and gastrointestinal infections in infants and young children), and seasonal coronaviruses. “Air detection of viral pathogens within airports and other international points of entry may represent an important component of layered surveillance systems for future pandemic preparedness,” the authors wrote. “Detection of respiratory pathogens through air monitoring may inform targeted mitigation strategies, including enhanced ventilation, air purification, public health messaging, and allocation of public health resources,” they wrote. Quick takes: Cautious optimism on Ebola, rare New World screwworm in a horse, HIV alert in Fiji News brief Stephanie Soucheray, MA Topics Ebola New World Screwworm HIV/AIDS Viral Hemorrhagic Fever Yesterday, World Health Organization (WHO) Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, PhD, said, "We are now starting to see encouraging signs that we are gaining ground,” in the ongoing fight against the Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC). He explained that his optimism was cautiously rooted in the absence of new cases in South Kivu since May and a slowdown in cases in Ituri province. The epicenter remains North Kivu, where cases are “rising fast,” Tedros said. In the past two weeks, weekly case counts have doubled in North Kivu, from 100 to 200 per week. Tedros warned that North Kivu is an area of very high population mobility and said much more work is needed to be done before the outbreak is contained. For the first time in more than 60 years, New World screwworm has been detected in a ranch horse in Texas, according to an update yesterday from the US Department of Agriculture’s Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service (APHIS). The case was detected last week in Presidio County. The parasite was found on the hind limb of the animal. So far this year, the parasitic fly has been detected in 49 animals in Texas and New Mexico. The archipelago nation of Fiji has declared an emergency now that one in 60 adults has HIV. The outbreak was first announced in January 2025, when the country had 2,016 new diagnoses of HIV. Last year, 59 babies were born with HIV acquired from their mothers. The emergency was declared because only 39% of people with HIV in Fiji know they are infected, officials said. The crisis is fueled in part by intravenous drug use and heavy drug trafficking on the islands. supplementary_news.content: ___ Market Information Top Poultry Companies Expert Insights Blogs Regions Magazines Sign In Poultry Meat Egg Poultry Health Sustainability Poultry Future Chicken Marketing Summit Poultry Tech Summit Broilers & Turkeys Diseases & Health Avian Influenza Another Minnesota turkey flock hit by avian flu The commercial flock of 55,700 birds is Minnesota's 13th case of highly pathogenic avian influenza this year. Roy Graber September 17, 2026 Big Dutchman Article Summary A commercial turkey flock in Big Stone County, Minnesota, has been confirmed with highly pathogenic avian influenza, marking the 13th case in Minnesota and the fourth in September 2026. The outbreak affects 55,700 birds and continues to spread across Minnesota, South Dakota, North Dakota, Wisconsin, and into Canada. A 55,700-bird turkey flock in Big Stone County, Minnesota, tested positive for HPAI on September 15, 2026 This is the 13th commercial poultry flock infected with avian flu in Minnesota so far this year Minnesota, South Dakota, North Dakota, Wisconsin, and Canada have all reported confirmed HPAI cases in commercial poultry The virus has spread across multiple border states, with Canada reporting one infected flock in Manitoba Avian flu continues to pose a significant threat to the poultry industry across the Upper Midwest region A commercial meat turkey flock in Big Stone County, Minnesota, is the latest case of highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) to be confirmed in the United States. The case was confirmed Sept. 15, and the affected flock included 55,700 birds according to the United States Department of Agriculture (USDA) Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service (APHIS). This is the 13th commercial poultry flock in Minnesota to be struck by HPAI so far in 2026, and the state's fourth case in September. The other three flocks were in Becker, Otter Tail and Wright counties. So far this fall, APHIS has listed only three states as having confirmed cases of HPAI in commercial poultry: Minnesota, South Dakota and North Dakota. However, earlier this week the Wisconsin Department of Agriculture, Trade and Consumer Protection reported that the virus had been detected in a commercial poultry flock in Barron County. APHIS has not yet released any information concerning that situation. North of the border, Canada has had only one commercial poultry flock infected with HPAI, confirmed in De Salaberry, Manitoba. All of the affected states and provinces share a border with Minnesota. Topics & Projects Antimicrobial Stewardship Chronic Wasting Disease Osterholm Update Podcasts Newsletters About CIDRAP CIDRAP in the News Our Staff Our Director Osterholm in the Press Shop Merchandise Contact Us About Search Support Menu Avian flu detected in Minnesota turkeys, US waterfowl News brief September 17, 2026 Stephanie Soucheray, MA Topics Avian Influenza (Bird Flu) Share Myles Tan / Flickr cc The US Department of Agriculture (USDA) Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service (APHIS) noted three major H5N1 avian flu outbreaks at Minnesota facilities this past week. Two commercial turkey operations in Big Stone County and Becker County had 55,700 and 44,400 birds affected, respectively. A commercial poultry breeder facility in Otter Tail County also reported an outbreak hitting 18,000 birds. In the past 30 days, 16 confirmed flocks have tested positive for highly pathogenic avian influenza, including 10 commercial flocks and six backyard flocks. Roughly 400,000 birds have been affected. Multiple wild-bird detections in Indiana, Utah In other APHIS news, wild bird detections have increased this month, with almost 30 detections in Kootenai County, Indiana, and 20 detections in Webber County, Utah. Other states have also noted a smaller number of cases. All recent wild bird detections are in mallards or other waterfowl. Airport air sampling captures COVID, influenza viruses News brief September 17, 2026 Mary Van Beusekom, MS Topics COVID-19 Influenza, General Lya_Cattel / iStock Air sampling at four US airports in 2023 and 2024 detected SARS-CoV-2, the virus that causes COVID-19, in over 98% of samples and influenza A in over 17%, according to a study published in PLOS Global Public Health. Researchers from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention led the study, which involved air monitoring in congregate areas at San Francisco International Airport, Newark Liberty International Airport, Washington Dulles International Airport, and Dallas/Fort Worth International Airport. The team placed samplers on tables 28 to 30 inches above the floor near customs and immigration inspection areas and international arrivals. Each ThermoFisher AerosolSense unit collected air samples for 10 hours per day, and the sample-collection cartridges were removed after 20 hours of use Monday through Thursday and 30 hours over the weekend. Correlation of the air samples with aviation wastewater, traveler nasal swabs, and national clinical surveillance data was also tested using data from two airports. Air sampling complements wastewater monitoring, the researchers said: “This approach is particularly effective for capturing respiratory pathogens from diverse populations, including asymptomatic or pre-symptomatic individuals who might not otherwise engage with clinical testing or contribute to accessible wastewater systems.” May be a component of pandemic preparedness Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) testing revealed SARS-CoV-2 in 98.3% of 463 air samples and influenza A in 17.2%. While influenza A positivity correlated with that in aviation wastewater, traveler nasal swabs, and national clinical surveillance, SARS-CoV-2 positivity didn’t align well. Detection of respiratory pathogens through air monitoring may inform targeted mitigation strategies, including enhanced ventilation, air purification, public health messaging, and allocation of public health resources. Genetic sequencing of SARS-CoV-2 from air samples identified lineages also found in wastewater samples during the same period from the same airports. In addition, it detected 30 viral species and recovered high-quality genomes for SARS-CoV-2, influenza, bocavirus (a virus that mainly causes respiratory tract and gastrointestinal infections in infants and young children), and seasonal coronaviruses. “Air detection of viral pathogens within airports and other international points of entry may represent an important component of layered surveillance systems for future pandemic preparedness,” the authors wrote. “Detection of respiratory pathogens through air monitoring may inform targeted mitigation strategies, including enhanced ventilation, air purification, public health messaging, and allocation of public health resources,” they wrote. Quick takes: Cautious optimism on Ebola, rare New World screwworm in a horse, HIV alert in Fiji News brief September 17, 2026 Stephanie Soucheray, MA Topics Ebola New World Screwworm HIV/AIDS Viral Hemorrhagic Fever Yesterday, World Health Organization (WHO) Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, PhD, said, "We are now starting to see encouraging signs that we are gaining ground,” in the ongoing fight against the Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC). He explained that his optimism was cautiously rooted in the absence of new cases in South Kivu since May and a slowdown in cases in Ituri province. The epicenter remains North Kivu, where cases are “rising fast,” Tedros said. In the past two weeks, weekly case counts have doubled in North Kivu, from 100 to 200 per week. Tedros warned that North Kivu is an area of very high population mobility and said much more work is needed to be done before the outbreak is contained. For the first time in more than 60 years, New World screwworm has been detected in a ranch horse in Texas, according to an update yesterday from the US Department of Agriculture’s Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service (APHIS). The case was detected last week in Presidio County. The parasite was found on the hind limb of the animal. So far this year, the parasitic fly has been detected in 49 animals in Texas and New Mexico. The archipelago nation of Fiji has declared an emergency now that one in 60 adults has HIV. The outbreak was first announced in January 2025, when the country had 2,016 new diagnoses of HIV. Last year, 59 babies were born with HIV acquired from their mothers. The emergency was declared because only 39% of people with HIV in Fiji know they are infected, officials said. The crisis is fueled in part by intravenous drug use and heavy drug trafficking on the islands.
